title: A Better Way To Build Organizations
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez argues that organizations designed around titles and reporting lines reveal little about whether they have the capabilities their work demands. She proposes designing around skills, then layering a strengths-based lens on top, drawing on Don Clifton's CliftonStrengths idea. Skills tell you what the organization needs; strengths tell you how to deploy people so they are energized and sustainable. She lists the payoffs, including better hiring, fuller use of existing talent, faster adaptation, clearer growth paths and lower burnout, and honestly names the costs: messier structures, the need to really know people, and ongoing reassessment. She suggests piloting the approach with one team or project.
points: Org charts tell you who reports to whom but almost nothing about whether you have the capabilities needed.
Skills-only designs risk draining people, and strengths-only designs risk energized people doing work that does not matter, so the two lenses need pairing.
Benefits include hiring for impact, using hidden talent, adapting faster, clearer growth paths and reduced burnout.
Costs are messier structures, the need for real conversations with people, and continual reassessment.
Start small with one team or project and share findings with decision-makers.
quotes: Most organizations design themselves around titles and reporting lines. You’ve got your directors, your managers, and your specialists and coordinators, all stacked in boxes on perfectly curated org charts.
As a recap, operating from a skills-based lens means obsessing less about roles and more on the skills and capabilities required to execute the organization’s goals and needs.

It’s important to note that when we use lean too heavily into skills without considering strengths, we risk placing technically qualified people into roles that end up draining them, resulting in disengagement and low morale.

They use the people they already have more effectively. Many organizations are sitting on untapped talent and potential because they’ve never taken the time to understand what skills their people harness beyond what’s outlined in their job descriptions. But a skills-and-strengths-based perspective allows you to tap into previously unknown capabilities while deploying them in a way that works for people.

It requires you to get to know people. To understand the skills your organization has, you need to have real conversations. Transactional relationships do little when it comes to unearthing people’s interests, passions, and talents. But when you take the time to get to know them, showing genuine curiosity in who people are and developing deeper connections with them, you open up considerable possibilities.
Designed with intention, these are the organizations that have figured out how to stop choosing between people, purpose, and profit, and instead deliver all three.
